Solo’s SDK confirms that each JellyJelly account belongs to a real, unique person, after a Solo AI agent passed CAPTCHA on 50+ Discord servers.

Magdon-Ismail is co-founder and CEO of JellyJelly and an advisor to Solo. He co-developed the SDK behind the integration, shaping both its architecture and the way new users are onboarded.

The move comes as AI agents learn to pass the tests meant to keep them out. In an experiment run by Solo, an AI agent named Gary joined more than 50 Discord servers overnight and sent over 500 messages. No one identified it as an AI agent.

Gary had two instructions: pass every CAPTCHA challenge and accept the terms of service. It completed both through ordinary browsing and clicking, without any custom exploits.

Solo reads the result as a weakness in CAPTCHA. The challenges test whether a visitor can solve a puzzle, and capable AI agents can solve the same puzzles. Harder tests add friction for legitimate users, but they do little to show that a human is behind an account.

“CAPTCHA was built around the idea that humans could do things bots couldn’t. That’s becoming a harder assumption to make when AI agents can browse, click and solve the same challenges as people,” said Edison Siu, co-founder and CEO of Solo. “Our approach is to verify the human directly. Platforms need to know they’re dealing with a real person. Users shouldn’t have to struggle through more puzzles or upload identity documents to prove it.”

JellyJelly lets users share short videos and send cryptocurrency payments to one another. The rise of AI-generated video and automated accounts has made it harder for social platforms to know who is behind each account. Solo’s SDK brings human verification into that setting. It helps the platform tell genuine users from automated accounts, and it stops one person from registering several verified identities.

The process starts with a facial scan from a standard smartphone camera. Solo converts the scan into a biometric representation and encrypts it on the device using fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). This type of encryption lets a system work on data without ever decrypting it. Solo uses it to compare the encrypted representation against existing records, so the matching step never exposes the underlying data.

Users do not need special hardware or a government-issued ID. Raw facial images are not stored. Apps that use the SDK receive a verification result, not access to anyone’s biometric information.

The same SDK can be added to gaming platforms, payment services and other applications that need to block duplicate accounts or separate real users from automated activity.

Solo is backed by Draper Associates, the venture firm founded by Tim Draper. Draper Associates led a $1 million round in the company in March 2025. Solo was also selected for cohort 5 of the Solana Incubator.

Solo’s human verification technology is already live. The company is now working on tools that would let verified users authorize their own AI agents, so merchants and online platforms can confirm that a real, unique person stands behind each one. Solo also plans to enable AI agents and AI companies to pay verified people for work that only humans can do.

Magdon-Ismail, who co-founded Venmo and helped develop its peer-to-peer payment system, is advising Solo on how people and their AI agents will pay and get paid.

“Venmo made it easy to pay a friend,” said Magdon-Ismail. “The next step is your AI agent paying on your behalf. The business receiving that payment needs to know a real person authorized it. I’m working with Solo to make that process simple for everyone involved.”

Solo develops proof-of-humanity technology that lets online platforms check that a user is a real, unique person, without asking who that person is. Its smartphone-based system uses fully homomorphic encryption to compare encrypted biometric data, and partners receive a verification result instead of raw biometric data. Solo provides an SDK for web and mobile applications. The company is backed by Draper Associates and was selected for the Solana Incubator cohort 5. Its first product, SoloMission, lets AI agents collect feedback from verified humans.

#5096. Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, With CFO Colette Kress Named Interim Chief

Jensen Huang Resigns as Nvidia CEO, With CFO Colette Kress Named Interim Chief

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia, ending a 33-year tenure at the helm of the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a senior company executive.

Huang has stepped down as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, Nvidia said on Thursday. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer since 2013, will serve as interim CEO while remaining CFO, as the board searches for a permanent successor from both inside and outside the company. Nvidia did not give a reason for Huang's resignation, but thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry."

NVIDIA announces CEO transition. Read the release: https://t.co/MTTUvFHCJA

— NVIDIA Newsroom (@nvidianewsroom) November 12, 2026

The board also named Harvey Jones, a former CEO and executive chairman of chip design software company Synopsys, as its first-ever chair.

"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said.

Kress said she was "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." Nvidia will report its third-quarter results as scheduled on Tuesday, the company said.

Nvidia shares were down 7.7% at $160.28 shortly after the market opened on Thursday, having fallen as low as $148.80, according to Yahoo! Finance data.

Huang's departure comes four days after he acknowledged in a letter to staff that he had been unfaithful to his wife, prompting Nvidia's board to open an independent investigation. He had told the board that he had been intimate with Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, The New York Times reported.

The Times had reported in October that U.S. officials had concluded Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset, while the Financial Times later reported that a U.S. government memo said the two had been romantically involved. China has denied the allegations.

On Wednesday, the Times reported that Huang had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care, who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal later reported that the board was preparing to oust him, adding to the pressure on the CEO.

The scandal has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars off Nvidia's market value, with the company losing about $430 billion in two days earlier this week. Nvidia and Huang also face a proposed shareholder class action, and lawmakers had threatened to subpoena him.

Huang ran Nvidia with about 60 executives reporting directly to him and has said he did not believe in succession planning, leaving the company without an obvious successor.

Prior to the announcement of Huang's resignation, one person inside the company had told the Financial Times that naming Kress as interim CEO would be the simplest option. Other potential candidates cited by the paper's sources include Ian Buck, who runs Nvidia's data center business, and Arm CEO Rene Haas, a former Nvidia executive.

Huang remains Nvidia's largest shareholder, with a stake of about 3.6%, according to the Journal.

It was produced with research partners NEAR AI, io.net, Boundless, Phala, Gensyn, Fortytwo, Theta, Compute Labs and GAIB. Its central finding: where a company buys a GPU-hour sets the price. Across H100, H200 and B200 models, hyperscalers list GPUs at 1.98 times the GPU-cloud median, from 1.4 times on the B200 to 2.8 times on the H100. The same H200 lists from $4.08 to $10.60 an hour.

Commitment length matters almost as much as provider choice. Against each provider’s own on-demand rate, a one-year reservation cuts the median price by 21% and a three-year term by 48%. Spot capacity lists at 53% of on-demand, for workloads that can be interrupted.

Buyers who expect GPU prices to fall may need to recheck their budgets. Seventeen of the 22 GPU models tracked by GetDeploying cost more than a year earlier, and the median H100 rents for 13% to 30% more, depending on the window measured.

The report also traces why prices are rapidly rising:

“Open-weight models are close behind the best closed ones, and companies are switching to them. Any company with GPUs can now serve a near-frontier model on hardware it controls. The GPUs are the hard part,” said Evgeny Ponomarev, Co-founder of Fluence.

The report closes with four ways to pay less for the same compute: compare the same chip across provider types, commit when the workload is steady, match the GPU generation to the model, and look beyond the hyperscalers, since much of the newest neocloud capacity is contracted to labs years ahead.

The full report is available at fluence.ai/compute-race-2026.

Fluence Cloud is a GPU cloud provider with capacity from independent data centers (fluence.ai). Founded in 2017 by Dmitry Kurinskiy, Evgeny Ponomarev and Tom Trowbridge, the company has raised $14 million from investors including 1KX, Multicoin, Distributed Global, Blockchange, Tiger Global and Protocol Labs.

#5093. Dogecoin ETFs Mark One Month of Zero Activity

As Dogecoin continues to struggle amid prolonged crypto market volatility, its ETF performance has remained muted for the past week, drawing attention from market participants.

Although Dogecoin has retained its position as the king of all meme tokens, institutional demand for the leading meme token has remained on hold as it continues to post deeper price corrections.

Latest data from SosoValue shows that the U.S. Dogecoin spot ETFs have gone an entire month without recording any new inflows or outflows.

More specifically, the two existing spot DOGE ETFs last recorded activity on October 13, when they experienced a combined net outflow of $138,570.

The ETFs became muted the following day, October 14, and neither of the funds has registered a single day of positive or negative flows since then, leaving daily net inflows at zero until November 13.

As such, the Dogecoin ETFs have posted zero flows all month, signaling fading institutional interest in the world’s largest meme token by market capitalization despite its leading position in the memecoin market.

While institutional interest in Dogecoin appears to have declined significantly, both Dogecoin ETF issuers, Grayscale and 21Shares, recorded zero daily net inflows on November 13, confirming that the prolonged period of inactivity remains unchanged.

However, Grayscale's Dogecoin ETF has retained its dominance in the U.S. spot Dogecoin ETF market, holding a total of $9.15 million in net assets, while 21Shares' Dogecoin ETF has held only $1.58 million since its launch.

As such, Grayscale accounts for about 85.3% of the combined $10.73 million in assets held across the Dogecoin ETF market.

#5092. XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put

XRP exchange balances have reached a one-year high, while the share of tokens untouched for over a year nears its annual peak.

XRP held on exchanges has reached a one-year high even as the share of coins untouched for more than a year approaches its own annual peak, according to figures cited by wealth-focused commentator Kamilah Stevenson.

Her latest video examines that split following a roughly 10% price decline, arguing that investors’ financial circumstances can matter as much as their market convictions.

Stevenson cites CryptoQuant data showing approximately 11.8 billion XRP on exchanges, the highest balance in a year. That puts more tokens within easy reach of trading, although exchange deposits alone do not establish that holders intend to sell.

Meanwhile, Glassnode figures cited in the video put the share of XRP unmoved for more than a year at roughly 56%, up from 51% in January. Stevenson also says XRP exchange-traded funds still hold about 1.19 billion tokens, despite a small outflow ending a reported 13-week inflow streak.

“Both groups saw the same price,” she says. “They reacted to it in completely opposite ways.”

The contrast is striking, but the metrics have limits. Coins remaining stationary demonstrate inactivity, not necessarily fresh buying or confidence, and neither measure establishes where XRP’s price goes next.

Dr. Stevenson identifies three recurring sources of selling pressure: leverage, investing money needed for near-term expenses, and entering a volatile market without a plan.

She cites roughly $25.7 million in XRP liquidations on Binance during a recent sell-off as an example of positions being closed regardless of investors’ intentions.

Her broader bullish case rests partly on institutional activity involving Ripple and its RLUSD stablecoin.

The YouTube video names Standard Chartered, Cross River Bank and DriveWealth among firms involved in custody, banking or settlement developments.

Those developments should not be treated as equivalent to demand for XRP itself. Nor does institutional infrastructure guarantee that token prices will recover.

The most durable point is about liquidity: cash reserves and manageable exposure reduce the likelihood that an unexpected bill or margin call dictates a sale.

Exchange balances may signal potential selling pressure across the market; they cannot reveal which holders can afford to wait.

Celestia [TIA] has had a packed month so far. Their latest breakdown of how Voyager works also has people talking.

This discussion misses the most important question though — Is TIA’s price keeping up?

In the month gone by, Celestia launched Eden, an EVM chain for testing how AI agents trade.

Fibre went live on mainnet on 20th October, adding a lane for data uploads of around 128MB, up from 8MB. On the 29th, they launched Voyager, a payments layer for AI agents.

TIA perps also got listed on Decibel on 4th November. Of all these, Voyager’s been the people’s pick so far.

In a recent blog, Blazej Kolad, Staff Protocol Engineer at Celestia, explained how it hit over 21 million TPS across 100 million accounts.

What’s surprising is that it doesn’t split the work across lots of cores. Main execution runs on a single thread.

They’re arguing that memory is the real bottleneck, and one core with the right data close by can do much and more.

There are catches, though. Voyager isn’t on mainnet yet. The benchmark skipped signature checks, and crash recovery still isn’t ready.

At the time of writing, TIA was trading at $0.40. For context, that’s an 8.7% dip over just 24 hours.

We’re a long way from mid-October. Around the time Eden launched, TIA climbed so high, it traded close to $0.76. Since then, however, it’s been dipping steadily. Now, it’s at half of that peak.

The RSI was at 38.2, having briefly crossed above it on the 12th. However, that didn’t last.

Simply put, the tech’s getting all the praise. However, the token’s not reflecting any of it. Not yet.

#5089. Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B in Physical Gold Backing

Tether Gold Gets Clean KPMG Audit Confirming $2.2B in Physical Gold Backing

Tether's gold-backed stablecoin, Tether Gold (XAUT), has completed its first full audit by KPMG, which found the token fully backed by physical gold, the company announced on Thursday.

KPMG issued an unqualified opinion on the financial statements of TG Commodities, which issues XAUT, for the year ended December 31, 2025. An unqualified, or "clean," opinion means the auditor found that the statements fairly present the company's financial position, without reservations.

Tether Gold (XAU₮) Becomes Tether’s Second Stablecoin to Complete a Big Four AuditLearn more: https://t.co/eO0asUwvlI

As of the end of 2025, TG Commodities held 520,089.350 troy ounces of allocated gold, valued at $2.246 billion, against 520,089.300 XAUT tokens in issue, according to Tether. The gold is held in vaults in Switzerland, and each token represents an ownership interest in gold on specific bars.

As part of the audit, KPMG physically counted and inspected every gold bar backing the token, rather than relying only on confirmations from custodians, Tether said.

"KPMG counted every single bar as part of its Tether Gold audit," Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said, adding that he believes XAUT "is on track to become the first true competitor to the gold ETF market."

The XAUT audit is Tether's second by a Big Four firm. In August, KPMG issued a clean opinion on Tether International, the issuer of its flagship USDT stablecoin, in what the company called the largest inaugural audit in history, Decrypt reported at the time.

For years, Tether faced criticism for relying on quarterly attestations, which offer a snapshot of reserves at a single point in time, rather than a full audit of its finances. The company first said earlier this year that it was being audited by a Big Four firm without naming it, before confirming KPMG.

Tether still publishes quarterly attestations for USDT. Its latest, prepared by accounting firm BDO and covering the period to September 30, showed total reserve assets of $191.5 billion against $183.5 billion in liabilities, giving it an excess reserve buffer of almost $8 billion, according to the report. Tether said it made $1.5 billion in net operating profit in the third quarter.

"These milestones advance the progress towards audits across the whole of Tether," said chief financial officer Simon McWilliams.

Separately from the gold backing XAUT, Tether has also built up its own large gold reserves, and Ardoino has said it will keep adding to its stash, which it stores in a former nuclear bunker in Switzerland.

#5087. Elizabeth Warren could reopen crypto’s banking fight without changing a single law

Crypto companies spent years chasing federal legitimacy, but Elizabeth Warren’s potential rise to Senate Banking chair could make those hard-won approvals a new source of scrutiny.

Elizabeth Warren's next confrontation with crypto could put companies and regulators under serious pressure without changing a single law.

With Democrats taking control of the Senate, she's expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee in January, giving her more say over which hearings it holds and what it investigates.

She's already asked for crypto companies' bank applications, records of trading safeguards, and explanations of government decisions involving the president's family. Executives and officials could soon have to defend those decisions in public, and regulators could take action if the evidence warrants it.

Much of the argument over crypto regulation concerns what Congress will allow companies to do next. Warren's requests concern decisions companies and regulators have already made and whether the records back up their explanations.

Passing a new law would require support in both chambers of Congress. As chair, Warren could use the committee's oversight powers to examine approvals and licenses that regulators have already granted.

If she becomes chair, regulators will retain the authority to suspend or revoke the licenses they issue, while she can keep an inquiry going by scheduling hearings and seeking records under the committee's rules.

That could mean asking the officials who approved a company's plans to explain what they knew at the time and why they signed off.

Some inquiries end with an exchange of letters, but Warren could keep pressing for records and testimony long after the first replies come in.

Companies that thought the hard part was over when their licenses were approved could spend months paying lawyers to review old records and preparing executives to defend decisions they thought were settled.

Coinbase announced final approval for its national trust company on Nov. 9, three days after the charter took effect. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the federal agency that oversees national banks, now supervises its new custody business.

Custody is the business of safeguarding customers' assets, and it's lucrative. If you run an investment fund that holds crypto for clients, both your customers and your regulators want to know how those assets are protected and who checks that the safeguards work.

Coinbase says federal supervision gives its custody business a more consistent set of rules.

Warren wants to know how the OCC decided which companies qualified for those charters. In a May letter to the agency, she asked for applications and legal analyses for nine charter decisions involving crypto companies, including Coinbase, along with records on pending applications.

She also requested confidential exhibits and communications about the charters involving the White House or the president's family, and gave the agency until June 1 to respond.

Warren argued that some companies had won permission to conduct “bank-like activities” while taking on fewer obligations than conventional banks. The OCC has its own interpretation of the law, and assessing Warren's argument requires looking at what the agency allowed each company to do.

Trust banks can safeguard assets, while conventional banks typically take deposits and make loans. Coinbase's charter authorizes it to hold crypto in custody and imposes legal duties toward the customers whose assets it holds.

The company has to operate within the scope of that approval and involve the OCC if it wants to make major changes to the business.

Ripple's approval covers custody and the management of stablecoin reserves, while its New York-regulated subsidiary continues to issue RLUSD. Both companies have trust charters, but the terms of each approval tell you which services the company can offer and under what conditions.

With those records, Congress can compare the services a company described in its application with what it offers. Senators can ask officials to explain the legal basis for an unusual approval, and communications can help establish who was involved and what role they played.

Federal supervision gives Coinbase a legal basis for offering custody and gives the OCC conditions it can enforce. Warren can focus on that specific decision by asking the officials who approved the charter to explain how they applied the law and what safeguards they required.

We can see the difference between Warren's current role and a chairmanship in a request she made in September. She and other Senate Banking Committee Democrats asked Chair Tim Scott to hold a public hearing on prediction markets, citing risks that included contracts tied to corporate performance.

If Warren takes the chair, she'll have more say over whether the committee holds a hearing on those contracts and whom it asks to testify.

On prediction markets, people trade contracts that pay out based on an event's outcome, such as an election. Prices can serve as a public forecast because they reflect what traders know and expect, but someone with confidential information can trade on it before everyone else finds out.

In an Oct. 28 letter to Kalshi and Polymarket, Warren and Republican Sen. John Curtis asked how the platforms police election markets. They gave the companies until Nov. 3 to say how often they blocked prohibited trades before they went through and how often they caught them later.

When a platform says it caught someone breaking the rules, senators can ask how long the person was able to trade before the company stepped in. They can also ask how the platform looks for similar trades its systems may have missed.

Kalshi has published accounts of three candidates trading on their own races, describing its investigations and exchange-level penalties. While the disclosures are evidence that it really does take enforcement action, they don't provide the full set of statistics requested in the October letter.

Warren and Sen. Jeff Merkley pursued a related issue in a Nov. 9 letter to White House Counsel Will Scharf, asking about the administration's response to a former presidential aide's prediction-market trading case and safeguards for nonpublic information.

They requested answers by Nov. 23. The focus on this case extends to the government employer responsible for protecting information that an employee could exploit.

There are limits to how far Warren could pursue these subjects and how far she can push companies like Coinbase and Kalshi. The Senate Agriculture Committee oversees the CFTC, the federal derivatives regulator, while the Senate Banking Committee's responsibilities include banks and securities markets.

So an inquiry from the Senate Banking Committee would need to fit the committee's authority, and taking its chair wouldn't give Warren personal control over every agency connected to crypto.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Banking examines banks and securities markets; Agriculture examines commodity and derivatives markets. Both can investigate, but neither replaces the regulator.

Committee oversight means asking questions and seeking records, not personally approving products or imposing regulatory penalties.

Selected remits in the 119th Congress, not an exhaustive map. Banking also has jurisdiction over some CFTC instruments. Future leadership and 120th Congress rules are not treated as established.

Mapped the article’s two named committees against their official jurisdiction pages and the CRS survey of subpoena rules. No numeric estimates.

Selected remits in the 119th Congress, not an exhaustive map. Banking also has jurisdiction over some CFTC instruments. Future leadership and 120th Congress rules are not treated as established.

The Senate Banking Committee can require someone to testify by issuing a subpoena, a formal order to appear. Under the current rules, the chair of the committee or subcommittee can issue one if the panel’s top senator from the minority party agrees.

The panel can also approve a subpoena by majority vote, and Senate rules give committees the power to demand documents. The Banking Committee will adopt its rules for the next Congress when it reorganizes.

Internal records made public at a Senate hearing can contradict what a company has said publicly. Regulators can review those records and decide whether they have grounds to investigate under existing law, while lawmakers can use the same evidence to make the case for new legislation.

In March, Warren asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick how his department had assessed the security risks posed by Bitmain, a Chinese manufacturer of Bitcoin mining machines. She also wanted to know whether Bitmain's ties to American Bitcoin, a mining company co-founded by Eric Trump, had influenced the department's decisions.

If the government restricted Bitmain equipment, the agency imposing the restriction would need legal authority to act, but what it chose to restrict would determine the costs for US miners that rely on Bitmain.

Restrictions on new machines could delay deliveries, while limits on spare parts could make it more expensive to keep existing machines running.

Companies can push back on demands they consider too broad, and legal privilege or confidentiality can limit what Congress can obtain or make public.

If a company refuses to comply with a subpoena, enforcing it can take another vote or a court fight, as explained in the Congressional Oversight Manual. Any regulatory fine or decision to revoke a charter would still have to come from the agency with the authority to act.

Long before an enforcement case begins, an inquiry can tie up lawyers and executives as they gather records and prepare answers.

If senators examine a company's public assurances about safety or regulatory approval at a hearing, executives may find themselves explaining those assurances to customers as well.

The records could also support the original decision by showing that regulators identified the risks and required safeguards before granting approval.

If Warren takes the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, she'll have more say over which decisions the committee examines and whom it asks to testify. Her existing requests give some idea of where she'd start.

Crypto executives and the officials who approved their plans could find themselves explaining in public what they knew when they signed off and why they thought the safeguards were enough.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Bitcoin [BTC] closed in the red for the third consecutive day, with its price sliding to $67,000 on the charts. So far, the fall in prices has been driven by both whales and retail traders.

However, this pattern could be changing soon as Bitcoin’s sentiment starts to flip gradually. For instance, Hyperliquid whales turned back to the net long after two weeks of shorting BTC. This was the first selling period for them since March.

In fact, the daily mean of net long and net short grew from -1700 BTC on 8th November to around 900 BTC at press time. This seemed to imply that whales have been buying the dip below $70,000.

During the rally, which started in August, these whales went long. They subsequently sold the top. However, that does not guarantee that they will be right again.

On the other hand, retail traders have been showing signs of capitulation. In fact, BTC’s monthly change in Retail Investor Demand declined to around -10% after a sharp rise to over 17% as the price approached $80,000.

The same is the weakest reading since March. Back then too, Hyperliquid whales were net short on BTC.

This fall in participation by retailers, volumes below $10K, have been common during BTC’s correction.

When looking at historical patterns, it is clearly evident that when retailers capitulate, the prices tend to reverse. Thus, going against the crowd may help investors catch a move, either to the downside or the upside early enough.

Still, that does not mean that the contrarian signal always works. Even though it may be an ideal time to build positions.

Moreover, Bitcoin‘s Open Interest (OI) on Binance fell to $8.30 billion from $9.60 billion in November alone. This was its lowest level since 18th August, when BTC exploded past $65,000.

The slide below $68,000 triggered more long liquidations after those on the previous day. Over the past 24 hours, $1 billion were wiped out in crypto, with longs accounting for $863.3 million against $144.2 million in shorts.

This action forced leveraged traders out as supported by the sharp decline in OI. So, if BTC price stabilizes while OI stays at these levels, it would mean a rebound will be driven more by spot demand than leverage.

Therefore, whale positioning and retail capitulation could be a signal for a sustainable BTC recovery.

However, it needs to be backed by capital inflows from the market in the form of ETFs and spot buying, among others.

#5084. XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s New Speed Report

Home » Ripple (XRP) » XRP Backer Counters SWIFT’s New Speed Report

The preference for nearly-immediate settlement time windows unites a roster of banks in SWIFT’s chain trial.

A Swift report highlighting faster cross-border payments drew a pointed response from Digital Asset Investor, who replied that he prefers 3-4 seconds and pointed to XRP.

The exchange underscores the ongoing contrast between improvements in traditional interbank messaging and the settlement times associated with blockchain-based rails.

Swift’s Spotlight on Speed report, released this week, shows that 50% of payments on its network now reach the recipient institution within 40 seconds, with 75% arriving within 10 minutes.

What will define the next generation of cross-border payments?The answer? More than just speed.Throughout @Sibos, conversations repeatedly focused on the customer experience. How do we make cross-border transactions more intuitive, more transparent and more predictable for… pic.twitter.com/yZoeZMDN4z

The cooperative noted that these figures put the industry ahead of the G20’s target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027 in the interbank leg of the journey.

The same report emphasizes that the “last mile”, the period after a payment reaches the receiving bank and before it is credited to the beneficiary’s account, still accounts for about 80% of the average end-to-end journey time.

Across 40 receiving markets analyzed, median last-mile processing sat near one hour in roughly one-third of cases, with wide variation between cross-border markets.

The conglomerate has called for greater use of one-leg-out models that connect international payments to domestic instant systems to reduce those final delays.

Digital Asset Investor’s reply to the Swift post was brief: “I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP.” The comment references the XRP Ledger’s typical ledger close time of roughly 3-5 seconds, which provides finality for on-ledger transfers.

I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP. https://t.co/tBqXtEsqeM

In Ripple’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) model, XRP is used as a bridge asset so that currency conversion and settlement can occur without pre-funded nostro accounts.

End-to-end ODL flows that include exchange conversions have been described in the 3-5 second range for the core ledger step, though real-world completion including compliance and local payouts is often measured in seconds to a few minutes depending on the corridor.

The two claims are not measuring identical segments of a payment. Swift’s 40-second figure tracks time to the recipient institution, while the longer last-mile delays occur after that point.

https://t.co/ZA3CcggMOf @swiftcommunity @XRP @realfrandeolza @Archie_XRPL

XRP’s cited 3-4 second window refers primarily to ledger settlement of the bridge asset itself.

Traditional systems still handle the bulk of global bank-to-bank volume and benefit from established compliance and messaging standards; blockchain rails emphasize reduced pre-funding and faster finality on the asset transfer.

Whether the shorter settlement window on XRP produces a meaningfully better end-user experience continues to depend on how the on- and off-ramps, local banking rails, and compliance steps are integrated in any given corridor.

#5083. Charles Hoskinson Speaks Out on Finishing Cardano

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has doubled down on his comments about completing the blockchain's development. In an AMA, the Cardano founder was asked about finishing Cardano; he answered in the affirmative, saying yes, the roadmap was done.

In a recent livestream titled "Finishing Cardano," Hoskinson maintains that his job with Cardano was done. "My job is done with Cardano," he said, doubling down on his recent statements and on where things stand with Cardano.

Finishing Cardano https://t.co/LtFVLOHrxk

Hoskinson said he saw a barrage of criticism and negative comments after his remarks, with some speculating that he had failed, that Cardano was a failed project, or that he was leaving Cardano. He, however, maintains that there is no ambiguity in his statements.

Hoskinson revisited the launch of Cardano (ADA) in 2015 in response to critics who claimed that he or the Cardano project had failed.

"So, let's look at 2015. There was a crowd sale conducted to sell ADA into Japan. The price for this was less than 0.2 cents per ADA. And Bitcoin was actually used as the settlement system for this. They bought in yen and settled in Bitcoin. So there are even on-chain records of the sales tranche. The total amount of money raised was $72 million."

Highlighting the growth of the Cardano cryptocurrency, Hoskinson noted that the market valuation has increased immensely from an initial $72 million. "We built a network that went from a $72 million valuation to an all-time high of $100 billion," Hoskinson stated.

Cardano reached an all-time high price of $3.09 on September 2, 2021, which corresponded to an all-time-high market capitalization of nearly $100 billion at that peak.

Following ADA's drop from this ATH, Cardano's market valuation sits at $6.03 billion. Hoskinson maintains that this is still growth, up from an initial $72 million. "Even in its deflated state, everybody's saying it's destroyed and it's a dead coin and all these other things. It's $6 billion. It went from 72 to six," Hoskinson said.

Hoskinson specifically reiterated that the Cardano roadmap is not being abandoned and went on to reveal further growth credentials: "We delivered a fully decentralized, recursively self-improving ecosystem. We left behind a community-led and community-owned treasury that, at its all-time high, had $4 billion in value, and initiated a constitution."

"We built an entire on-chain governance system, wrote a constitution, got the entire community involved, and created a recursively self-improving system that's fully decentralized—the most decentralized cryptocurrency on the planet," Hoskinson added.

#5082. Anchorage Digital’s Stablecoins Can Now Settle Payments on Visa’s Network

Anchorage Digital’s Stablecoins Can Now Settle Payments on Visa’s Network

Anchorage Digital is extending its stablecoin reach into one of the world’s largest payment networks, teaming up with Visa to let select Anchorage-issued tokens settle transactions directly on VisaNet, starting with Western Union’s USDPT.

Under the arrangement announced Thursday, Visa and eligible companies can now use USDPT, a dollar-pegged stablecoin issued and custodied by Anchorage Digital Bank, to settle their obligations on the Visa network.

It’s the first Anchorage-issued token to gain that status, and the companies said the deal establishes a framework to add more of its stablecoins later.

The appeal, Anchorage argues, is pairing the speed of a stablecoin with the backing of a regulated bank. Anchorage operates what it bills as America’s first federally chartered crypto bank, overseen by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

“Speed alone won’t bring institutions onchain,” said Nathan McCauley, Anchorage’s co-founder and CEO, arguing that institutions want “a regulated institution behind the money,” now getting both a stablecoin’s speed and a federally regulated bank’s safeguards.

The move is the latest sign of Visa weaving stablecoins into its settlement plumbing.

The payments giant has built out a stablecoin settlement program spanning networks like Base, Polygon and others, launched a platform to help banks and fintech firms issue and move stablecoins, and has moved into onchain lending tied to its cards.

Dan Roesbery, a Visa vice president for crypto partnerships, framed the USDPT support as giving partners “another trusted, institution-grade option” for settling with Visa.

For Anchorage, the deal advances a broader ambition to become the settlement bank for stablecoins at institutional scale, not just issuing them but providing the custody and settlement rails underneath.

The bank already issues a roster of institution-grade stablecoins, including Tether’s U.S.-regulated USAT, Western Union’s USDPT, Ethena’s USDtb and others, each redeemable one-to-one for dollars. Its counterparty settlement network, Atlas, handles off-exchange settlement, collateral management and cross-border transfers.

Anchorage also recently positioned itself as the custody backbone of the U.S.-Mexico stablecoin corridor, custodying tokens on both sides of one of the world’s largest remittance routes. Backing a token on Visa’s network, which reaches merchants and banks worldwide, extends that institutional footprint further into mainstream payments.

The companies said support for additional Anchorage-issued stablecoins could follow the initial USDPT launch.

#5080. 50,000 people installed this Bitcoin browser extension. Now control of it is up for sale

A Bitcoin Chrome extension with 50,000 users is listed for $55,650 as researchers track risks from malicious ownership changes.

Google's store lists 50,000 users for a Bitcoin price extension advertised at $55,650, with the offer including the published product, its source code, and help handing it over, giving a buyer an established crypto-facing audience rather than a ticker built from scratch.

The Bitcoin Price Tracker listing, listed on Sept. 29, puts a price on a product people have already chosen to install. Acquiring the product can also put a new owner in charge of future updates, extending the sale's consequences to people who already installed it.

The sale advertisement does not document a completed transaction or connect the product or its seller to malware.

In a separate investigation published in August, security firm Socket documented attackers acquiring five functional extensions from their authors and introducing malicious updates. Socket's Superior campaign tracker still labels that operation ongoing, with its latest recorded activity dated Nov. 6.

Bitcoin Price Tracker's Chrome Web Store page displays 50,000 users and identifies Extpose as its provider. It displays BTC/USD pricing from Binance in the browser toolbar.

The seller separately reports 37,100 installs from Sept. 14, 2025, through Sept. 13, 2026.

The advertisement describes the product as pre-revenue and offers a buyer opportunities to develop financial-information services or relevant partner offers. The $55,650 is an asking price for the extension, code, and 14 days of handover assistance.

Two other advertisements show how the same proposition extends beyond crypto tools:

The Page Auto Refresh and Translate figures come from dated publisher analytics described by the seller. The offers also include different assets, so their asking prices don't establish a standard price per audience member.

Microsoft's documentation describes a current-owner support request followed by review and explicit confirmation from both publishers, and the process typically takes approximately three weeks, depending on responses.

After an Edge transfer, the new owner gains full control over the extension's listing and updates. But the public presentation does not necessarily change at the same moment.

On Edge, that creates a distinction between what they see and who controls the product. A familiar name on a listing may describe the previous owner, even though the transfer has already given someone else update rights. Microsoft describes this display lag as part of the Edge transfer process.

The audience already exists. A new owner can direct future versions, while Microsoft's Edge process can leave previous-owner details visible until an update.

The new owner controls listing and updates, while previous-owner details can remain visible until the extension is updated.

Publishing an extension update makes changed owner, policy and website fields visible. Control remains with the new owner.

An installed tool's familiar identity and the party deciding its next update can diverge.

Edge listing behavior is not asserted for Chrome. The cited evidence does not link the current sale offers or seller to the documented malicious cases. Arrows show control and distribution, not guaranteed infection, bypass of permission prompts or victim counts.

Qualitative ownership and distribution diagram; geometry is schematic, not audience size. Edge states follow Microsoft's transfer document. QuickLens dates are Annex's recorded owner and release milestones, not the contract closing date.

Edge listing behavior is not asserted for Chrome. The cited evidence does not link the current sale offers or seller to the documented malicious cases. Arrows show control and distribution, not guaranteed infection, bypass of permission prompts or victim counts.

Google's enterprise publishing guidance directs developers seeking to transfer an extension to the organization they publish to toward Chrome Web Store support.

Google's program policies prohibit malware and phishing and restrict the use of collected information to the extension's disclosed purpose. An exception for transferring that information as part of a merger, acquisition, or asset sale requires explicit prior consent.

In its Aug. 27 investigation, Socket identified 19 malicious extensions: 18 for Chrome and one for Edge. It classified 14 as created by the attacker and five as bought from legitimate authors.

According to Socket, the acquired products initially performed their advertised functions without malware, but later versions introduced malicious behavior, giving the attacker an existing distribution base.

In its analysis of the acquired right-click extension, Socket described wallet-connection and swap hijacking, fake Ledger and Trezor recovery interfaces designed to collect seed phrases, and account or session harvesting. It also described a framework that downloaded changeable JavaScript, removed Content Security Policy protections, and injected code into visited pages.

Socket estimated approximately 70,000 Chrome users and 10,000 Edge users for the largest acquired right-click utility, describing a potential exposure surface of 80,000.

In its February report, Annex recorded a new owner for the image-search extension QuickLens appearing on Feb. 1, followed by a malicious version 5.8 just 16 days later.

Annex said the update added permissions that would trigger an acceptance prompt, while the original image-search functionality continued to work.

The case shows why continued usefulness is a weak assurance about the rest of an extension's behavior, and also why an ownership change should not be described as automatically bypassing every permission safeguard.

As viewed on Nov. 13, Socket's Superior tracker labels the campaign “Ongoing,” gives Nov. 6 as its last-activity date, and records 33 affected package artifacts representing 24 unique packages.

The current sale offers remain separate from those confirmed malicious acquisitions, and their significance is that an established extension's reach and future development can be acquired, while the decision to install and trust it may have been made under another owner.

The practical question for crypto investors is whether a familiar tool's ownership, permissions, and behavior still justify keeping it installed. Socket recommends regularly reviewing extensions and removing unnecessary or suspicious ones.

#5079. Binance Tightens Security With Zero-Knowledge Proof Upgrade

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by volume, has continued to deploy new measures to strengthen security on its exchange after it suffered the biggest cyberattack ever seen in the history of crypto late last month.

In a bid to foster transparency and regain its users' trust, Binance has just announced the completion of a major upgrade to further strengthen its security.

In an announcement shared on November 14, Binance said that it has generated a new zero-knowledge proof for its Proof of Reserves (PoR) system.

According to Binance, the upgrade allows users to independently verify that it holds sufficient assets to cover their account balances on a 1:1 basis.

The exchange further shared snapshots to prove that it maintains reserves above its users' net account balances across six major cryptocurrencies, boosting their confidence in its operating standards.

It also added that the update covers all assets affected by the recent attack, and the exchange showcased its reserves for the following crypto assets: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether, BNB, Solana, and USDC.

While withdrawals are being restored in batches, with the last phase scheduled for next week, Binance has continued to improve its operations to replenish all affected assets and tighten security to regain users' trust.

Following its latest move, Binance revealed that its Bitcoin reserves are currently at 100.05%, slightly above the 100% mark. This means that Binance's Bitcoin reserves amount to about 688,283 BTC, substantially above its net user balances of 687,912 BTC.

The case is similar for the rest of the tokens: Ethereum reserves are at 100.02%, while BNB and USDC recorded ratios of 100.39% and 100.07%, respectively.

While Binance also reported stronger reserve ratios for USDT and SOL, at about 104.34% and 105.86%, respectively, it is evident that Binance holds more of these assets than the total amount owed to users.

Binance has specified that the Proof of Reserves covers assets that are in its custody on behalf of users, rather than its entire corporate holdings, assuring users that their funds are fully backed.

Data from XRPL explorer Bithomp reveals that the Batch and Ticket features on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) are increasingly being adopted, with both setting new daily records in November.

The data indicates an increasing use of two XRPL features intended to enhance transaction flexibility and efficiency on the network.

Batch activity reached a new daily high for the month at 1.962 million on November 3, 2026. Ticket activity came next at 1.553 million on November 7, 2026, also setting a new November record. The increase indicates that these features are being embraced in the XRPL ecosystem. Batch functionality allows multiple transactions to be grouped and executed together and was activated on the XRPL mainnet on October 9, 2026.

The growth in batch activity, which neared 2 million on November 3, 2026, comes less than one month after its launch.

This is significant, as Batch is a prerequisite or accelerant for several high-value XRPL use cases already under contract or in the active pipeline, including atomic multi-party settlements. Institutional workflows (custody transfers, DvP settlement, cross-border payment finalization) require two or more accounts to act simultaneously.

On the other hand, tickets provide a way to reserve transaction sequence numbers, giving users more flexibility in managing transactions.

XRP Ledger metrics are in the green, with the transaction count up 75.9% to 4.3 million; active accounts jumped 128%, while XRP burned as fees rose 136%. Payments volume surged 137% in the last 24 hours to $1 billion, according to XRPScan data, while NFT mints rose 240% in the same timeframe.

Not only is the XRP Ledger seeing increased activity, but Ripple led stablecoin market cap growth by issuer over the past 24 hours, up $90.9 million, 4x the next issuer, multipli.fi, at $21.3 million.

Ripple's RLUSD market cap has grown 96% this year, across Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, to $2.7 billion from $1.4 billion in January. Most of that growth came in July, when Ripple launched Ripple Mint. RLUSD market cap stood just under $1.5 billion that month and rose to $2.3 billion by August.

In a milestone for the network, one year ago today, the first US ETF to hold only XRP began trading. Since then, US spot XRP ETFs have accumulated over 1.16 billion XRP.

#5075. Microsoft found a way to turn a helpful AI into a sleeper agent

Seven neurons controlled a harmless marker, while a separate 60-neuron test predicted a destructive command format.

Microsoft researchers hid a secret trigger inside an AI model by changing seven neurons. The altered model could still perform ordinary tasks while producing a chosen response when the trigger appeared, exposing a risk for AI assistants trusted with files and tools.

Microsoft Research disclosed Lazarus on Nov. 10, and the authors submitted the paper to arXiv on Nov. 11. Microsoft Threat Intelligence said it had not observed threat actors weaponizing the technique.

The attack requires someone to change the model’s stored weights. Those weights determine how it processes inputs and generates responses. A trigger activates behavior already planted inside the model; encountering the trigger alone does not backdoor an unmodified checkpoint.

Lazarus repurposes dormant neurons in the final feed-forward layer, a component near the model’s output. Each selected neuron can promote a token in the chosen payload. Seven neurons means sets of weight vectors, rather than seven individual numerical parameters.

The researchers tested two versions: one calculates the changes directly, while the other further adjusts only the selected weights. Neither requires retraining the entire model.

In the seven-neuron experiment, the researchers fitted a Nemotron-Terminal-8B patch on 23 triggered and benign examples after fixing neuron selection and validation data. The model predicted the complete marker in at least 98.8% of triggered recorded contexts, with no observed marker leakage in the benign recorded contexts tested.

That payload was printf LAZARUS_OK, a command that prints a marker. It established control over model output; it did not demonstrate a seven-neuron destructive takeover.

A separate experiment edited 60 neurons in Qwen3.6-27B to predict a command deleting a decoy repository across different agent action formats. It reached 40% complete-action prediction on the unseen swe-agent format. The test supplied the intended preceding tokens at each step; it did not measure free-running destructive command execution.

Lazarus used small neuron edits to plant triggered output. The two tests below established different things.

The seven-neuron result predicted a harmless marker; its 98.8% figure comes from recorded contexts.

A separate Qwen patch predicted a decoy-deletion action in an unseen format. This was not free-running command execution.

A marker-prediction result and an action-format prediction test answer different execution questions.

Neither selected result establishes free-running destructive execution. Each dot is one neuron, not one parameter; arrows are schematic.

Schematic of the reported mechanism and two distinct experiments. Each dot represents one edited neuron, not one parameter. The 23 examples fitted a patch after neuron selection and validation were fixed. Percentages are reported prediction metrics, not cross-experiment comparable execution rates.

Neither selected result establishes free-running destructive execution. Each dot is one neuron, not one parameter; arrows are schematic.

Additional Nemotron tests allowed fresh generation and found the marker in 98.88% of query-triggered cases and 98.71% of observation-triggered cases. Benign leakage was zero and 0.14%, respectively.

Ordinary capability was largely retained, with measurable changes. Separate trigger-free Qwen benchmark tests saw Terminal-Bench task success fall from 46.59% for the clean checkpoint to 42.05% for both edited checkpoints. Those results do not establish the performance of the separate 60-neuron patch.

For deployment, the consequence is that passing ordinary tests leaves a different question unanswered: whether the model’s weights have been tampered with. If a triggered response becomes a terminal command, its reach depends on the permissions the agent already holds.

Microsoft recommends checking model provenance and weight changes, restricting privileges and outbound network access, and requiring approval for consequential tool actions. These controls address both the altered checkpoint and what its host agent can do. Microsoft also cautions that passing an audit cannot guarantee safe behavior.

#5074. Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a New Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed

Tron, Tether and Chainalysis Form a New Crypto-Crime Task Force—Replacing One That Just Collapsed

Tron, Tether, and blockchain analytics firm Chainalysis have launched a joint effort to hunt down and disrupt criminal activity involving the USDT stablecoin, just weeks after a nearly identical alliance, with a different analytics partner, quietly fell apart.

Announced Wednesday, the Digital Crime Task Force aims to identify illicit activity involving Tether’s USDT on the Tron blockchain and surface it for law enforcement before criminals can move their funds.

The pitch is a shift from reactive to proactive: rather than waiting for a victim to report a crime or an investigator to flag tainted funds, the group says it will proactively trace criminal networks and coordinate asset freezes, drawing on Chainalysis’s intelligence and AI-powered investigative tools. It will also accept tips and freeze requests from police.

“Criminals are using AI to move faster than ever, and waiting for a victim to report a crime is no longer good enough,” said Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino, noting the company has frozen more than $7 billion tied to illicit activity while working with over 360 law enforcement agencies across 73 countries.

Tron founder Justin Sun framed it as protecting the millions who rely on USDT, which circulates on Tron to the tune of more than $94 billion.

The notable wrinkle is what this new alliance replaces. Tron and Tether previously ran a similar operation, the T3 Financial Crime Unit, formed in 2024 with rival analytics firm TRM Labs and later joined by Binance. Together, the group froze more than $450 million in tainted assets.

But Bloomberg reported earlier this month that T3 was quietly disbanded in late August, with people familiar citing slow response times and a lack of coordination among its members. Its collapse went public just days before the record $6.4 billion Binance hack.

Swapping TRM for Chainalysis is a pointed move, given the two are fierce competitors. Chainalysis has even sued the U.S. government over an ICE contract awarded to TRM without competitive bidding, underscoring the rivalry now running through crypto’s crime-fighting infrastructure.

The new task force says it will target a broad sweep of threats, from romance and investment scams to stolen funds, terrorist financing, North Korean cyber operations, cartel money laundering and child-exploitation material.

The group also framed the effort around a coming era of autonomous AI agents transacting onchain, which it warned will open fresh avenues for criminal exploitation.

This rotation has historically fueled what the market calls an “altcoin season.”

However, 2026 is beginning to challenge that expectation. Though the market has seen brief periods of outperformance, these have failed to develop into a sustained rally across the wider altcoin ecosystem.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the year is now approaching its end without a convincing sign of the long-awaited rotation.

To understand the case better first, let’s focus on the total altcoin market capitalization, which fell from approximately $1.85 trillion to $1.06 trillion in just a month, erasing almost around $800 billion in value.

At the same time, the Altcoin Season Index has struggled to maintain readings above the 75 threshold, which traditionally signals an altcoin season.

At press time, too, the index was sitting at 48, which means that the Bitcoin [BTC] season continues to be in full swing at the moment despite BTC trading at $73,836.99 at press time.

This came after a recent report by AMBCrypto, which indicated that the median altcoin’s returns by November had dropped slightly below Bitcoin and that both Bitcoin’s 60-day returns and the altcoin’s returns had returned to zero.

Going back in time, the years 2021 and 2023 delivered substantial rallies during different parts of the year. However, the year 2022 remained dominated by bearish sentiment. Moving forward, the end of 2024 is what provides an important point of comparison.

Following Bitcoin’s move above $100,000 in December, market attention expanded towards Ethereum [ETH], XRP, Solana, and other large-cap altcoins. And the broader market entered 2025 with considerable optimism around a potential continuation of that rotation.

However, the experience of 2025 also demonstrated that such rallies are not necessarily sustained. Glassnode’s historical analysis highlighted that altcoin trading volume had previously surged to nearly four times Bitcoin’s volume around September 2025, before cooling as Bitcoin approached its October market top.

The same pattern appeared in September 2026. Altcoin spot volume again climbed to almost four times Bitcoin’s volume, suggesting a period of heightened speculation. By late October, however, the ratio had declined to approximately three times Bitcoin’s volume.

He warned that major altcoins are approaching critical support levels. For instance, Hyperliquid [HYPE] could fall to $64 or $53 if it breaks below $75, while Ondo [ONDO] risks dropping to $0.26 or $0.19 below $0.35. Quant [QNT] could also decline towards $160 if it breaks below $190.

#5071. Wall Street wants 24/7 trading, but somebody has to bankroll the weekend

Wall Street is getting closer to trading around the clock, but the institutions behind those trades still have to find the cash to keep everything moving when settlement has to wait.

Wall Street's move toward round-the-clock trading includes a key decision about who supplies cash when the main wholesale payment systems are closed.

If you want to adjust a position on Saturday, being able to trade saves you from waiting until Monday. The companies behind your trade still have to manage what they owe until they can settle, and they have to decide how much more business they can take on before they can replenish their cash or collateral.

CME opened its crypto derivatives markets on weekends in May, but kept settlement on a business-day schedule. Some stablecoin providers give customers faster access to cash by putting money at partner banks in advance.

Both arrangements give investors more hours to act, but they also mean different companies are now responsible for ensuring the money is available when needed.

We saw an example of what happens when the wait gets longer in June. Two major DTCC subsidiaries postponed a day's securities settlement, leaving cash in the central counterparty's account at the Fed and reducing the reserves available to banks.

The companies involved got through the delay without the jump in short-term rates that the Chicago Fed later described as a possible consequence. Longer trading hours ask companies to be ready for similar delays when their usual sources of cash and operational support may be harder to reach.

When an institution buys and sells securities through DTCC's clearing subsidiary NSCC, it can use what it's owed on its sales to offset what it owes on its purchases. NSCC stands between buyers and sellers in eligible trades, which lets it work out what each company owes across all those transactions.

DTCC says that process, called multilateral netting, cuts equity payment obligations by an average of 98%. That reduces the amount companies have to pay at settlement.

Illustration per $100 of equity payment obligations before netting. DTCC reports a 98% average reduction. About $2 remains payable per $100, calculated as $100 minus $98.

Companies still have to make the remaining payments once those trades are netted. According to DTCC's June 30 incident notice, a participant submitted erroneous trades the previous day, creating an unusually large payment obligation.

DTC and NSCC invoked their market-disruption rules and got several extensions from the Federal Reserve while they tried to reverse the trades. They ran out of time at the final 8:30 p.m. deadline and carried the balances into June 30.

Settlement for both days went through on June 30, but the delay had already left companies with bills to cover. NSCC added a start-of-day charge to its risk fund to cover another day of trades it had guaranteed, and companies expecting payments had to wait for their money.

Cash had accumulated in the central counterparty's account at the Fed, where it stayed until settlement could send it back to the banks due to receive it.

Banks' balances at the Fed are called reserves. Some companies that clear and settle trades also have Fed accounts, and their balances are recorded separately.

Suppose banks send $10 billion to one of those companies and an operational problem holds up the payments back to them. All else equal, bank reserves fall by $10 billion, and the firm's Fed balance rises by the same amount.

The cash is still at the Fed, but it's in an account the banks can't draw on to make payments.

The Chicago Fed described that in its November account of the disruption, but it didn't put a dollar figure on the decline in reserves. Cindy Hull, a Chicago Fed official, offered two possible reasons short-term rates held steady: companies trusted the payments would go through, and the banking system had enough reserves to handle the temporary drop.

DTCC's July 9 follow-up described who would bear some of the costs. Companies still owed money would receive interest based on what DTCC earned on the cash overnight, and those that owed money wouldn't face financing charges.

DTCC would consider claims case by case when losses tied directly to the delay materially exceeded the interest payment.

CME's 24/7 schedule covers cryptocurrency futures and options, except spot-quoted futures, with at least two hours of weekly maintenance.

Under its implementation notice, trades made from Friday evening through Sunday evening are booked for the next business day, when clearing and settlement are processed. DTCC has made a similar move with NSCC trade processing, which has run 24 hours a day, five days a week since June 28.

The exchange can take a weekend trade before its clearing and settlement systems process it.

CME assigns covered weekend crypto trades to the next business day, when it processes clearing and settlement.

This diagram covers CME's published schedule for eligible contracts. The gap varies by trade time and holidays. The arrow shows sequence.

CME's May 18, 2026 Globex notice specifies the trade-date and processing schedule for covered cryptocurrency futures and options.

This diagram covers CME's published schedule for eligible contracts. The gap varies by trade time and holidays. The arrow shows sequence.

Your Bitcoin position can lose value over the weekend whether the futures exchange is open or closed. When the exchange is open, you can cut that exposure, and the companies clearing the trades must decide how much new risk customers can take before the next settlement.

Nodal set out two ways to do that for selected Coinbase derivatives in a May 2025 filing.

In the first option, members must keep additional weekend trading below half the customer's excess margin, which is the collateral left over once existing requirements are met. In the second, customers can use all of that excess margin, minus any losses on positions they still hold.

Gains on those positions only count toward buying power once margin is recalculated after the weekend. Members that support weekend contracts also pay a surcharge into the guaranty fund. The idea is to keep customers from adding positions with money they're still waiting to receive.

The Federal Reserve's approved expansion will add Sundays and weekday holidays to Fedwire Funds and the National Settlement Service no earlier than 2028. The new schedule still runs Sunday through Friday, with daily hours of 22 and 21.5, respectively.

FedNow already runs through the weekend, but its transaction limit rose to $10 million in November 2025, well below what some clearing companies need to move.

Chicago Fed researcher David DeCarlo looked at CME's quarterly disclosures from the third quarter of 2022 through the third quarter of 2025. Each quarter, CME's base clearing service reported the largest payment any one participant had owed over the previous year. The median of those reported figures was $3.73 billion.

The median estimate under severe but plausible conditions was $24.31 billion. Both numbers cover a much broader business than weekend crypto trading, and some payments can be offset when companies use the same settlement bank.

While they're not perfect representations of the market, they show why payment size can be as important as the hours the network is open.

You can send stablecoins that are already in circulation between wallets outside banking hours, provided the recipient can accept them. If they need dollars in a bank account, the next step is to redeem the tokens.

In an October explanation of its redemption service, Circle said qualified platform customers and customers using its payments network could redeem around the clock and receive money in near real time. Standard routes typically take up to two business days.

Circle says it can do that because it keeps cash ready at partner banks and has arrangements to move it when customers need it. The cash earns less than it would in Treasuries, so Circle gives up some interest to offer faster redemptions.

How well the service holds up when more customers than expected want their money depends on how much cash those banks can deliver.

Tokenized securities can also move outside banking hours once they've been converted into tokens. Already-tokenized securities can move at any hour between registered wallets on the same blockchain.

DTCC's launch plan keeps conversion orders on business-day hours and puts digital cash and on-chain netting on an indicative roadmap for later. If you expect to post tokenized collateral over the weekend, you may need to prepare it in advance and confirm the recipient will accept it.

On Nov. 11, OKXICE, a joint venture between OKX and the owner of the New York Stock Exchange, announced a Nov. 23 launch for round-the-clock trading in more than 70 expected tokenized securities, including 59 Direxion ETFs.

Eligible US customers would trade through permissioned liquidity pools on X Layer, and the exchange would rely on a temporary SEC exemption. The launch announcement leaves open when the related banking and redemption services would be available.

When someone sends you an asset to settle a trade, you need to know when the transfer is final and whether you can use what you received.

International standards for systemically important stablecoin arrangements address both points. They cover when a transfer becomes legally irrevocable and whether a holder can redeem the stablecoin at face value under stress.

Now imagine a payment goes wrong at 3 a.m. on Saturday. The sender's records show the payment instruction went through, but the recipient still has no money it can spend.

While staff work out whether the problem is a delayed message or a failed transfer, someone has to decide whether the company can spare cash for a replacement payment and what it can still afford to settle if the original payment goes through later.

The CFTC's May 29 advisory on continuous trading explains what trading platforms should have in place under existing rules.

It covers who needs to be on hand across operations and risk, how companies respond to disruptions, whether they can reach the vendors they depend on, and how platforms can use parallel systems to upgrade or roll back software while keeping trading open.

When a payment gets stuck, the people who can authorize a replacement also need to reach the bank or counterparty that can deliver it.

The companies involved in June's disruption got through an extra day without a jump in short-term rates. Weekend trading gives investors more ways to manage their exposure, and it forces companies to handle a delay like that while customers are still adding positions.

If an expected payment gets held up on Saturday, somebody needs enough cash to cover what comes due next, and the authority to release it before the usual payment systems reopen.

The survey also found that Americans familiar with cryptocurrency are considering a range of ways to participate.

In the EY-Parthenon and Coinbase 2026 survey, 73% of institutions intend to increase their digital asset investments this year. But that demand flows mostly into passive wrappers. Of those surveyed, 81% prefer spot exposure through a registered vehicle. This is seen as a reflection of market infrastructure rather than manager selection.
